newsitem.title: USA: Congress returns to budget, foreign policy debates.
newsitem.headline: Congress returns to budget, foreign policy debates.

text.p: The U.S. Congress returns this week from a one-week holiday with budget, trade and campaign finances on the agenda, but Republican leaders put the brakes on plans for quick passage of spending and tax cut bills.

The ambitious schedule that called for Congress to pass these bills by July 4 will be slowed to give more time for debate of these massive changes to domestic programmes and tax laws, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Friday.

One of the first items lawmakers must resolve is the $5.5 billion disaster relief bill they failed to deliver before leaving town on the Memorial Day holiday. The bill provides aid to the flood-ravaged upper Midwest and other states and another $1.9 billion to pay for U.S. troops in Bosnia and the Gulf.

Republicans refused to back down when threatened with a presidential veto over an unrelated provision that would bar a government shutdown this fall. The action left them open to solid political punches from Democrats and President Bill Clinton and divided their own party with some key members supporting a compromise to guarantee disaster relief.

"There are three big issues which still have yet to be determined that could prompt a veto," House Appropriations Committee chairman Bob Livingston said last week. The Louisiana Republican opposed as "an overly simplified solution" the idea being pushed by his party's leaders to prevent a government shutdown for one year. Clinton has said he would veto the disaster bill with this provision.

"We would expect to finish that bill very quickly upon our return and hopefully our leadership will either work out their differences with the president on the big ticket issues, or else we'll go through the veto dance," Livingston said.

As they departed May 23 loose ends were left to be tied in the five-year balanced budget agreement that passed both the Senate and House in May with strong bipartisan support. Minor differences in their separate versions remained and final action was expected within the week after the session resumes.

Exalting in the latest reports of the buoyant U.S. economy, Vice President Al Gore urged Congress to quickly approve the budget and enact the legislation necessary to carry out its tax and spending goals.

"We must continue on this steady, prosperous course by reducing the deficit ... On behalf of the president, I want to call on Congress to keep growth alive and pass our balanced budget plan when members return to Washington," he said at a White House news conference on Friday.
The House on Wednesday opens debate on a major foreign aid reauthorization bill that contains provisions to tighten sanctions against Cuba.
Congress has not passed a foreign aid authorisation bill since 1986, and leaders of both parties hope they have crafted a bill that will please a majority.

Contentious debate is also foreseen over President Clinton's decision to extend for another year Most Favoured Nation trade status with China. The decision sparked objections from Clinton's top Democrat in the House, Richard Gephardt of Missouri.

During the first week of June, the Senate continues work on a Republican plan that allows employers to offer time off instead of overtime to hourly wage workers. The administration and most Democrats oppose the idea.
Republican leaders had hoped to pass by July 4 bills to trim federal spending, primarily Medicare health care, and give taxpayers a $85 billion tax cut over five years.
Speaking in Georgia on Friday, House Speaker Gingrich said the sheer size of the undertaking made it probable they would miss the deadline.
"We're going to do everything we can to get it done by the fourth of July. But it may run a little bit longer than that," the Georgia Republican said.
